data.title: A journey to the Vikings 2013 – part 2: Gotland’s picture stones and rauks
data.excerpt: We continue the journey of discovery in search of the Vikings that our member Ľubka made in 2013. The second part takes in the large open-air museum at Bildstenar with the Hamar picture stones, the towering rauk formations of Langhammars, the Viking village at Stavgard and the stone-roofed fishing cottages of Holmhällar.

children.text: We continue the journey of discovery in search of the Vikings that our member — Ľubka — made in 2013. You can find the first part
here
Bildstenar

At BILDSTENAR there is also a large open-air museum in which the life of the inhabitants of Gotland is captured within one large complex. There are a kind of burgher houses here, and runestones with picture script that were found in the little village of Hamar. They are named after it, Hamar I–IV.
I was pleased that Hamar is such an important place. Ever since childhood I have had neighbours by the name of Hamár.
I walk past a unique windmill of the German type. This one catches my attention with its six sails, which I have not seen anywhere else.

The little houses are built according to period, from the oldest dwellings of the period of 700 BC up to the 18th century. There is already a water mill here as well, but what was interesting for me was the way in which tar was obtained in the past. Tar was an indispensable jointing material both in the building of Viking and other ships and of houses and other structures on dry land. Tar sticks, it does not let water through, it insulates well and it is readily available.

In the surrounding woodland on the rocks there are always plenty of conifers containing tar (resin). In a sort of oval stone with a hollow they made a hole in the middle and set it on a foundation of stones about 1.5 m high. In this way they made an artificial little cave (a small cellar), and beneath the hole in the rock they made a collecting vessel with a long thin trough (a channel) along which the melted tar ran.

On the oval stone they evidently laid wood, which smouldered slowly, and the tar, melting out of the wood, trickled down into this simple but ingenious system for further use. In the open-air museum there is a collection of carriages, tools and implements from the various crafts that the inhabitants of the island used in the past.

children.text: Raukomrade-LANGHAMMARS

In the afternoon we came to Raukomrade-LANGHAMMARS, a place by the sea where there are tall rock formations in the shape of heads, but also of all sorts of other shapes. It is magnificent. A few steps from the road we were as if in an enchanted stone land of giants…

Rauk (in Icelandic hraukr) is the Gotland word for a rock formation. There are a great many stones here on the sea shore whose soft limestone surface has weathered and been gnawed away by the sea, while the hard inner core has remained intact.

The weather is going our way, the sun is shining, and so each of us finds a place among the rocks and we relax. I dip my feet in the rock pools, where the water is pleasantly warm, but after a while I am already splashing about at the edge of the sea. A pleasant refreshment and a necessary wash, since we had no shower in the morning and it looks as though we shall spend this night too somewhere away from civilisation.

Not far away there is a typical Gotland fishing settlement in a bay with a large, pretty and spotlessly clean stone beach, which a great many tourists seek out. According to the information available, one can eat well here, but we did not get to enjoy any fish speciality, because all the little houses were already closed. But at least we feasted our eyes on another lovely place on Gotland.

children.text: We found a spot in a lonely place by a lake. We put up the tents, prepare supper and watch the sunset. The place is again very lovely; before going to sleep we go for a quick bathe in the freshwater lake with its crystal-clear water and shoals of tiny little fish.

Jindro lit a little fire and relaxed; for a moment Ivka and I disturbed him with our presence, but we did not want to be a nuisance. I felt a little sorry when in the morning some of the women said that they had sat there long into the night.

I, on the other hand, was up among the first. I cannot deny myself the sight of the dawn and the sunrise. For me it is like a magnet, when I see the little sun leap out of the water and carry on cheerfully on its daily round.

By the lake, travellers in two caravans had also settled down to sleep; otherwise there is only the murmur of the water, the song of the birds, and now and then we hear the noise of a car in the distance.
We come to STAVGARD (AMMUNDE)
near the town of Burs out of curiosity.

blocks.alt: A journey to the Vikings 2013 – part 2

children.text: There is a Viking village there, so we look round it. We came early; there is not a living soul anywhere – only the morning sun lights up the little houses exactly as it did a thousand years ago… But that does not bother us; we walk through the settlement – there is plenty to look at. Little houses as if out of a fairy tale, covered with thatch, and inside the primitive furnishings of a household: a sort of oven, a table with a bench and a bed with straw to sleep on. Under the roof they nailed up animal hides – certainly for insulation, but also, once dried, for further working. The implements and tools of the household farmer, a simple device for weaving – strips of leather (later threads) were plaited together with strips of fur, with the help of a sort of ring-shaped wooden weight at the ends of the strips, into one broad band, and from this warm winter clothing was probably sewn. Leather was used in every possible way; it was available, pliable, strong and durable, and the products made from it could be decorated according to the imagination and according to what the products served for. In the settlement there is one large communal hearth, a well for water and various utensils made, or adapted, from animal bones.

children.text: Holmhällar

Our next stop is at Holmhällar, a nature reserve, in the fishing village of Holms beneath more rocks of various shapes – rauks – with Skvalpiku on the other side. We arrive in the fishing settlement with wild hares leaping about not far from us. I find myself in another world – in the past, several centuries ago…

Above the settlement, in a good strategic spot, stands a sort of bunker for watching the sea, from which in the past they guarded every corner of the bay against intruders. Fishermen’s cottages covered with stone slabs on the roofs, with interestingly contrived chimneys (two hewn stones set on edge, covered by a further stone). The stone roof slabs are weighted down with further, smaller ones. Over the whole surface of the roof, smaller slabs are laid between the large ones so as to fill every crack.

Without any of the conveniences of civilisation, hidden far from other dwellings, undevastated by the 21st century, the little houses live quietly on, a life of their own. It is fascinating… Only we disturbed the peaceful atmosphere by passing through; otherwise there was not a soul.
